Body aches, sagging skin?

It’s not all in your head!

New research from Stanford Medicine reveals that our bodies go through two periods of rapid change, around ages 44 and 60.

Researchers found that thousands of our molecules and even the microbes living in us experience dramatic changes around these ages.

At around 44, changes in molecules were linked to cardiovascular disease and the ability to metabolise caffeine, alcohol and lipids. The researchers unsurprisingly linked this to perimenopause in women.

The second wave of changes happens around 60 and included molecules involved in immune regulation, carbohydrate metabolism and kidney function. Molecules linked to skin and muscle ageing changed at both time points

These changes aren’t gradual. They’re sudden, and they affect everything from metabolism and immune function to skin and muscle health.

So what does this mean for us? Pay attention to your health during these critical years. Simple lifestyle tweaks, like more exercise and less alcohol, can make a big difference!

If you’re struggling with weight gain in perimenopause, these 3 things could be sabotaging your efforts to lose it:

1. The Pendulum Effect: You over-restrict and the pendulum swings so far one way, until your will power runs out and you swing all the way over to the opposite side and overeat.

2. Not eating enough protein: I know I know, you hear this everywhere, but truly, protein is so important and you’re likely not eating enough. Recent research found the “Protein leverage effect” where due to muscle loss in perimenopause, the body requires more protein and when we don’t get enough protein, we tend to overeat on other foods to make up for it, which can  lead to weight gain.

3. Not eating enough fiber: research show that soluble fiber can reduce visceral fat by stabilizing blood sugar and increasing satiety making fat loss easier. Fiber is also essential for a healthy gut microbiome which supports fat metabolism and reduces inflammation.

Nobody talks about the grief in perimenopause.

Not grief for youth.

Grief for the version of you that felt capable without trying so hard.

The woman who could walk into a meeting, speak clearly, and finish a sentence without suddenly losing the word she was about to say.

The woman who could juggle work, kids, a messy house, and a million responsibilities… and still have patience left at the end of the day.

The woman who didn’t lie awake at 3:12am, heart racing, replaying a conversation she had six hours earlier.

The woman who didn’t feel irrationally irritated by the sound of someone chewing, breathing, or asking one more question.

The woman who could have a glass of wine at dinner and not wake up at 3am with anxiety buzzing through her chest.

The woman whose jeans fit the same way week to week… instead of waking up one day wondering when her waistline quietly changed.

The woman who felt sharp. Steady. Solid in herself.

And suddenly…

You lose your train of thought mid-sentence in a meeting.

You walk into a room and forget why you went in there.

You snap at your kids over something tiny and feel immediate guilt.

You reread the same email four times because your brain just won’t lock in.

You wake up tired no matter how early you went to bed.

And a small voice starts whispering:

What is wrong with me?

So many women think this means they’re becoming less capable.

Less resilient.

Less themselves.

But what’s actually happening is physiology colliding with a life that hasn’t slowed down.

And the margin you used to have… the one that let you handle everything… suddenly gets smaller.

So the same life…

feels heavier.

That grief you feel?

It’s not weakness.

It’s the recognition that you know exactly what you’re capable of.

And you refuse to disappear during the decade where your power, wisdom, and voice should be getting louder, not quieter.

I’d love to hear: does this resonate with you?

Nobody talks about the grief of perimenopause. And I think it’s time we did.

Grief for the body that used to respond the way you expected. Grief for the energy you used to have.

You don’t have to pretend you’re fine with all of this. You just have to know that on the other side of that grief, there’s a version of you that’s stronger, more self-aware, and more at home in her body than she’s ever been.

She’s waiting for you. But you have to let go of the old one first.

You’re phenomenal.

Even if you’re struggling right now.

there have been times in the perimenopause journey where I haven’t been able to recognise myself or my reactions.

snapping at my kids. losing my sh*t over things that would have never bothered me before. catastrophising my family’s safety on a regular Tuesday morning. not unusual.

for the longest time my strategy was to push the feelings down and power through. spoiler: that made me snappier, not calmer.

so now I do something different. it sounds almost too simple, but stay with me.

I stop.

I sink into my body and locate where the emotion is actually sitting. chest? throat? stomach?

then I name exactly what I’m feeling and describe it to myself. like this: “I’m feeling anxious. it feels tight, dense and sticky in my chest.”

and then, instead of running from that feeling, I focus on it. I just stay with it.

here’s why i love it so much: after a while, the feeling starts to fade. on its own. without me snapping, spiralling, or reaching for something to numb it.

there’s real science behind this - naming an emotion actually dials down the alarm centre in your brain and brings your thinking brain back online. psychologists call it “affect labelling.” I call it the “feel it” theory - because instead of pushing the feeling away, you actually feel it. and that’s what sets it free.

perimenopause can be a rollercoaster of emotions and feelings that can knock the wind right out of you - but this practice has been completely transformative for me. not because it makes the hormones disappear, but because it gives me a way to ride the wave instead of being dragged under by it.

try it next time a big feeling hits: stop, locate it, name it, describe it, stay with it.

then come back and tell me in the comments what you felt and where it was sitting - I read every single one.
